pos.personaBrief: Cullis's Wolves were a direct, fast-tempo side that wanted the ball moved forward quickly, not held: the sources quote him wanting every pass to be 'decisive and long rather than pretty and short' and describe a 'percentages game' of quick distribution from defence (Spartacus 1960; These Football Times). Possession was a means to an early, direct attack, not a goal in itself, so he rejects patient keep-ball play but values creating danger on the break.

pro.personaBrief: The most verified axis: Cullis asked for direct football ('every pass ... long rather than pretty and short', 'put the ball into the opponents' penalty-area ... in a maximum of three passes', Spartacus 1960) and his team drove long balls to wingers and a target centre-forward. Patient build-up and safe short play out from the back are against that model, and a free striker behind the defence is exactly the situation he wanted to exploit.

est.personaBrief: The sources show a fixed, drilled shape: wingers Mullen and Hancocks kept wide to supply crosses, and full-backs were 'instructed to find one of his forwards with the pass' (Spartacus 1960; These Football Times). That points to clear, rehearsed positions and a winger who stays on the touchline, while short combinations in tight spaces and a centre-forward dropping deep are not documented.

lar.personaBrief: The team's identity was wide: 'Wingers were very important to the way Cullis's team played', with Mullen and Hancocks crossing (These Football Times, verified). Crosses and wingers beating the full-back were the main route to goal, so the flanks are preferred over an extra central midfielder or central attacks.

blo.personaBrief: Cullis wanted fast recovery of the ball, 'rapid tackling by every player so that we obtain possession of the ball before the other side has it under control' (Spartacus 1960, verified), which supports immediate pressing after losing it. He did not favour sitting deep, and the 'tempo beyond the capacity of the other side' statement points to an attacking, high-intensity approach; a high defensive line or pressing from the first pass is not directly documented.

mar.personaBrief: Marking is a documented gap (openQuestions): no source describes Cullis's zonal or man system. This answer comes from general knowledge of English football of the 1950s, where man-marking with a clearly assigned opponent was the norm, plus the verified emphasis on clear, drilled roles (Spartacus 1960); it is not based on verified evidence about this profile.

pla.personaBrief: Cullis was a strongly identity-driven coach: his tactics 'demand that Wolves play at a tempo which is beyond the capacity of the other side' (statedView, 1960), and Ron Flowers in 1962 said 'our manager never sets out to copy the tactics of any other club' (Spartacus, verified). He imposed his method through hard training ('train until it hurts') and kept his plan rather than studying the opponent or abandoning his style against stronger sides.

res.personaBrief: Cullis explicitly framed football as entertainment: 'The primary duty of a team is to entertain the public' (statedView, 1960). He also won three league titles and two FA Cups, so results mattered, but his style of attacking, direct play and the 'percentages game' suggests he would not shut a game down to protect a narrow win or settle for a draw away from home.

sis.personaBrief: A drilled collective is central to his method: he wanted players who 'train until it hurts because it makes them better players on Saturday' and a 'percentages game' built on set patterns, and he described a system in which everyone does a defined job (statedView and Spartacus 1960). Star players are not exempt from the system, but the sources do not describe the stars being freed from it.

jog.personaBrief: This axis has no verified evidence (gaps.axes). From general knowledge of this profile: Cullis's Wolves were athletic and fit, with pace on the wings and high tempo, so physical intensity matters, while a classic number 10 who does not run has no real place in his team (his inside forwards like Broadbent were runners). Answers are kept consistent with the verified tempo and the 'train until it hurts' statement.

bas.personaBrief: Youth mattered to Cullis: he praised 17-year-old Peter Broadbent as one who 'could well develop into one of the outstanding inside-forwards of his day' (1950, verified) and released Johnny Hancocks to 'prepare for the future' (1957, verified). He built squads around the club's own players, but he was also a title-focused manager who wanted seasoned quality when it mattered, so he does not treat experience as secondary in the title race.

lid.personaBrief: Evidence is mixed: Cullis was demanding and disciplined ('I tell my players that they must train until it hurts', statedView), while Ron Flowers said he 'never adds to our worries at such a time by large-scale inquests' (1962, verified), suggesting calm management of people. He is firm about discipline applying to everyone, but the sources do not show him consulting senior players, so the people-versus-orders question is left neutral.
